Yuki: Hi everyone! The school festival is only three weeks away. We still haven't decided what our class will do. Any ideas?

Sora: I think we should open a food stall. A takoyaki stand is always popular, and we can earn a lot of money for the class trip.

Mei: Takoyaki sounds nice, but cooking needs a fire permit from the office, and we only have one week to get it. That might be hard. How about a haunted house instead? We can use our classroom and make it dark and scary.

Ren: I like the haunted house idea! But last year three classes did haunted houses, so it wasn't special anymore. What about a small café? We can sell drinks and cookies that don't need a fire permit, just an electric kettle.

Yuki: A café is safe and easy, but I want something more exciting. Let me suggest a game corner with a ring toss and a shooting game. Visitors pay 100 yen for three tries and can win small prizes.

Sora: Oh, I love the game corner! It's cheaper to prepare than food, and we don't need any permit. I change my vote to that.

Mei: Same here. The game corner is fun and safe. Let's do it!

Ren: Okay, I agree too. Yuki, can you write down our plan and show it to the teacher tomorrow?

Yuki: Sure! I'll prepare the paper tonight. Thanks, everyone. Let's make the best festival ever!

**Daiki:** Let's start at 3:30 instead. Hana, can you make it a bit earlier?

Greenwood University Dormitory posted the following report on its website.

**Dining Hall Satisfaction Survey: 2026 Results**

Last month, the Dormitory Office invited all 480 residents to complete an online survey about the dining hall. We received 312 responses, which is the highest number we have ever collected. Thank you to everyone who took part. Below is a summary of what we learned, along with the changes we plan to make.

When asked how satisfied they were overall, 58% of residents said they were "satisfied" or "very satisfied." This is an increase from 49% last year. However, satisfaction with breakfast was lower than satisfaction with dinner. Only 41% of residents said they were happy with the breakfast menu, while 67% were happy with dinner.

The survey also asked residents to choose the single change they most wanted. The most popular request was "more vegetarian options," chosen by 38% of residents. The second most popular was "longer opening hours in the morning" (29%), followed by "lower prices" (21%). The remaining 12% chose "other."

In the comment section, many residents wrote that the dining hall closes too early in the evening. At present, dinner service ends at 7:30 p.m., but a number of students with late classes or club activities said they often miss it.

Based on these results, we will make two changes starting next month. First, we will add two new vegetarian main dishes each week. Second, we will extend dinner service until 8:30 p.m. on weekdays. We are still studying the breakfast situation and welcome further feedback.

**Comments from residents:**

Mei (second year): I am really glad the office is extending dinner hours. I have a chemistry lab that finishes at 7:15, so by the time I reach the dining hall, the best dishes are gone and service is almost over. The extra hour will help students like me a lot. I think the food itself tastes good, but I wish breakfast started earlier, because my first class is at 8:00.

Daniel (third year): The survey results match what I hear from my friends. I am a vegetarian, so I am pleased that more meatless dishes are coming. In my opinion, though, the prices are still too high for what we get, and I am disappointed that the office is not lowering them. I rarely eat breakfast here, so the morning hours do not affect me much. Overall, I believe the dining hall is slowly getting better.

**Notice from the Greenfield Public Library**

The Greenfield Public Library will change its opening hours starting from September 1. We made these changes after asking 500 library users to complete an online survey in July. Below is a summary of the new schedule and two comments from regular visitors.

**New Opening Hours (from September 1)**
- Monday to Friday: 9:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. (previously closed at 6:00 p.m.)
- Saturday: 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. (no change)
- Sunday: now closed (previously open 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.)

In the survey, 62% of users said they wanted the library to stay open later on weekdays, mainly so that students and workers could use it after school or after work. At the same time, only 18% of users said they visited on Sundays, and many of them lived far from the library. Because so few people came on Sundays, we decided to close on that day and use our limited staff to keep the building open longer during the week. The reading room on the second floor will remain quiet at all times, but the first-floor study area will now allow group discussion until 9:00 p.m. We hope these changes make the library more useful for everyone.

**Comment from Mei, a high school student:**
"I think the new weekday hours are wonderful. I finish club activities at 6:30 p.m., so I could never use the library before. Now I can study here in the evening. The first-floor group study area is a great idea because my friends and I often want to talk about our homework together. However, I am a little sad about losing Sundays. My family used to visit together on Sunday afternoons, and now we cannot."

**Comment from Mr. Tanaka, a retired teacher:**
"For me, the most important thing is a quiet place to read, and I am glad the second-floor reading room will stay silent. I usually come on weekday mornings, so the closing time does not affect me. I understand that few people came on Sundays, but I worry about families who relied on that day. Perhaps the library could try opening one Sunday each month in the future."
question_data.subject: 英語

choices: Very few people visited on Sundays, so the staff could be used for longer weekday hours.
The library wanted to give its staff a full day of rest each week.
The building needed cleaning and repairs every Sunday.
Most Sunday visitors asked the library to close on that day.
questions.explanation: 正解は「Very few people visited on Sundays, so the staff could be used for longer weekday hours.」。本文に「only 18% of users said they visited on Sundays」「Because so few people came on Sundays, we decided to close on that day and use our limited staff to keep the building open longer during the week」とあり、日曜来館者が少なく、その分のスタッフを平日延長に回すためと説明されている。

62% of survey users wanted the library to stay open later on weekdays.
Opening one Sunday each month would be a good idea.

questions.explanation: 正解は「62% of survey users wanted the library to stay open later on weekdays.」。本文に「62% of users said they wanted the library to stay open later on weekdays」と調査結果の数値が事実として明記されている。他は Mei や Mr. Tanaka の意見・提案であり事実ではない。

question_data.passage:
Greenfield High School Student Council recently asked all 600 students about a possible change to the school uniform policy. At present, every student must wear the same uniform: a blue blazer, a white shirt, grey trousers or a grey skirt, and black shoes. Some students have said the rules are too strict, so the council carried out a survey from May 6 to May 13. A total of 480 students answered the questions. Below are the main results, followed by two comments from students.

Survey Results
- Should the school keep a uniform of some kind? Yes: 360 students (75%). No: 120 students (25%).
- Which change would you most like to see? More colour choices: 192 students. Permission to wear a school T-shirt in summer: 168 students. No change at all: 120 students.
- 70% of students said the current uniform is uncomfortable in hot weather.
- The most common reason given for keeping a uniform was that it saves time in the morning.

The Student Council will share these results with teachers next month. The council hopes the school will allow a school T-shirt during the summer term, because this was the change that received strong support and it would help with the comfort problem reported by many students.

Comment from Mika (Grade 11):
"I was surprised that most students want to keep a uniform. I thought everyone would want to wear their own clothes! Personally, I like having a uniform because I don't have to think about what to wear each morning. But I agree that the blazer is far too warm in July. I really hope the school lets us wear a light T-shirt in summer. That single change would make my school days much more comfortable, and I believe it is the best idea in the whole survey."

Comment from Daniel (Grade 12):
"To me, the survey shows one clear thing: students are not asking to get rid of the uniform, just to improve it. Most people, including me, voted to keep a uniform. What I want most is more colour choices, because grey is boring and I would prefer to choose between a few colours. I don't mind the heat as much as some students do, so the summer T-shirt is not my top priority. Still, I think it is wonderful that the council actually listened to us."
question_data.subject: 英語

choices: 480 students

questions.explanation: 正解は「480 students」。本文に「A total of 480 students answered the questions.」とあり、回答した生徒数は480人。600人は全校生徒数、360人は制服維持に賛成した人数、120人は制服に反対した人数なので誤り。

questions.explanation: 正解は「The uniform should offer more colour choices.」。Danielは「What I want most is more colour choices, because grey is boring」と述べ、最も望む変更が色の選択肢の追加だと意見を述べている。制服廃止は望んでおらず(keep a uniform に投票)、夏のTシャツは最優先ではない(not my top priority)と言っているので他は誤り。

choices: They want to remove the uniform policy entirely.
They decided not to report the results to teachers.
They ignored the comfort problem in hot weather.
They support allowing a school T-shirt in summer.
questions.explanation: 正解は「They support allowing a school T-shirt in summer.」。本文に「The council hopes the school will allow a school T-shirt during the summer term」とあり、生徒会は夏のTシャツ許可を支持している。制服の完全廃止は望まず、暑さの問題に対応しようとしており、結果は来月教員に共有すると述べているので他は誤り。

Greenleaf Online Academy ran an online course called "Practical English for Daily Life" from April to June. After the course ended, the school posted the results of a feedback survey on its website, along with two comments from students who completed the course.

Survey Results

Greenleaf Online Academy thanks the 120 students who answered our survey. The course had 16 lessons, each lasting 50 minutes. All lessons were held in the evening, and every lesson was recorded so that students could watch it again later.

When we asked which part of the course students liked best, 45 students chose the small-group speaking practice, 38 chose the recorded videos, 25 chose the weekly writing tasks, and 12 chose the live chat with teachers. We were happy to learn that 90 percent of the students said they would recommend the course to a friend.

However, some students told us about problems. The most common complaint, made by 52 students, was that the internet connection sometimes broke during live lessons. The second most common, made by 30 students, was that the lessons started too late in the evening. Based on this feedback, we have decided to move next term's lessons to the afternoon and to add a stronger backup system for the internet. We believe these changes will make the course even better.

Student Comments

Mia: I joined this course mainly because I wanted to speak more confidently, and the small-group practice was perfect for that. With only four students in each group, I had many chances to talk, and the teacher corrected my mistakes kindly. The recorded videos were also a great help. I work part-time three evenings a week, so I often missed the live lessons, but I could always watch them later at my own pace. My only wish is that the live lessons had started earlier, because by 9 p.m. I was already tired.

Tom: For me, the best part was definitely the writing tasks. I used to be afraid of writing emails in English, but after twelve weeks of practice, I can now write a clear message without using a dictionary. I think every learner should try this course. The teachers were friendly and quick to reply. The internet did cut out a few times during live lessons, which was annoying, but honestly the recordings solved that problem for me, so it never really bothered me much.

choices: The small-group speaking practice

Greenfield Community Gym recently posted the results of its yearly member satisfaction survey on its website, along with two comments from members.

Greenfield Community Gym — 2026 Member Satisfaction Survey

Thank you to the 480 members who answered our online survey last month. Here is a summary of what we learned.

Overall, 82% of members said they were "satisfied" or "very satisfied" with the gym. The most popular facilities were the swimming pool (chosen by 65% of members) and the weight-training room (chosen by 58%). The least used facility was the indoor running track, used by only 12% of members.

When we asked what members would most like us to improve, the top answer was "longer opening hours on weekends," chosen by 41% of members. The second most common request was "more group fitness classes in the evening" (33%), and the third was "newer machines in the weight-training room" (26%).

We also asked about our staff. A clear majority, 90%, agreed that our trainers were "friendly and helpful." However, only 55% felt that staff were "easy to find when needed." Because of this, starting next month we will add one extra staff member to the main floor every evening.

We will hold a meeting for all members on July 15 to discuss these results. We hope to see you there.

Member Comments

Aiko (member for 3 years): I come to the gym mainly to swim, so I was happy to see the pool is still the most popular facility. I usually visit on Saturday afternoons, and the gym closes too early for me. I think longer weekend hours would be the single best change the gym could make. The trainers are always kind, but I agree it can be hard to find someone when I have a question, so the new evening staff plan is a smart move.

Ken (member for 6 months): As someone who lifts weights, I was surprised that the running track is so rarely used — I think many members simply don't know it exists. The weight machines are getting old and sometimes make strange noises, which worries me a little. I'd rather the gym spend money on new machines than on longer hours. Still, I'd encourage every member to come to the July meeting and share their honest opinions.

questions.explanation: 正解は「The gym should spend money on new machines rather than on longer hours.」。これはKenのコメント「I'd rather the gym spend money on new machines than on longer hours.」を言い換えた個人の意見である。他の3つは調査の数値(90%・12%・480人)であり、ジムが報告した客観的事実なのでKenの意見ではない。

choices: Aiko wants newer machines, while Ken wants longer weekend hours.

Both members think the running track should be removed.
Aiko prioritizes longer weekend hours, while Ken prioritizes newer machines.
questions.explanation: 正解は「Aiko prioritizes longer weekend hours, while Ken prioritizes newer machines.」。Aikoは「longer weekend hours would be the single best change」と週末営業時間延長を最善とし、Kenは「I'd rather the gym spend money on new machines than on longer hours」と新マシンを優先している。選択肢1は両者を逆にしており誤り。トラック撤去には両者とも言及せず、Kenは7月の会合への参加を呼びかけているため、3・4も誤りである。

question_data.passage:
My First Cooking Class

Last spring, I joined my first cooking class at a small community center. I had never cooked anything before, so I was both excited and nervous. The teacher, Ms. Lee, was very kind. On that day, she chose a simple dish for us: vegetable curry. "Don't worry," she said with a smile. "Everyone makes mistakes at first."

We began by washing the vegetables. Then I started cutting the carrots and onions. My hands were slow, and the other students finished much faster than me. I felt a little embarrassed, but I kept going. After all the vegetables were ready, Ms. Lee told us to heat oil in a pot and add the onions.

Here is where my big mistake happened. I was so worried about being slow that I turned the heat up very high to catch up. Soon, the onions began to burn, and black smoke rose from my pot. The whole kitchen smelled terrible. I panicked and did not know what to do. Ms. Lee came quickly, turned off the heat, and helped me start again with a clean pot. This time, she stood beside me and told me to keep the heat low.

With her help, I cooked the onions slowly until they turned soft and golden. Then I added the carrots, water, and curry powder. The kitchen began to smell wonderful. When the curry was finally ready, I tasted it. It was delicious! I could hardly believe that I had made it myself.

At the end of the class, Ms. Lee gathered all of us together. She said, "Cooking is not a race. Take your time, and pay attention to each step." Those words stayed in my mind. I realized that my mistake came from rushing, not from a lack of skill.

Now I cook at home every weekend. I am still not perfect, but I never turn the heat up too high anymore. That first class taught me something important: being slow is fine, as long as you are careful. I am very glad that I did not give up on that smoky, difficult day.

Last spring, I had an experience that I will never forget. It taught me something important about kindness.

It happened on a rainy Saturday morning. I was on my way to the city library to return some books. As I walked along the crowded street, I noticed a small brown wallet lying on the wet ground near a bus stop. Nobody else seemed to see it, so I picked it up and looked inside. There was about 5,000 yen in cash, a student ID card, and a photo of a young girl with her family.

At first, I did not know what to do. I was already late for an appointment with my friend, and the library was still ten minutes away. For a moment, I thought about leaving the wallet at a nearby shop. But then I saw the name on the ID card: "Aya Mori, Sakura High School." I decided that I could not just walk away. I wanted to return it to her myself.

I went into a small coffee shop to get out of the rain and think. I remembered that Sakura High School was only two stations away by train. So I took the train there and asked a teacher at the front gate to help me. The teacher was very surprised and kindly called Aya to the office. When Aya arrived, her face changed from worry to joy. She told me she had been searching everywhere for the wallet, because the photo inside was the last picture taken with her grandmother.

Aya thanked me again and again. A few days later, she sent me a handwritten letter and a small box of cookies as a thank-you gift. Reading her warm words made me feel truly happy.

Before that day, I used to think that small actions did not really matter. But now I understand that even a simple act of kindness can bring great joy to someone. I learned that helping others is never a waste of time, and I hope I can keep this lesson in my heart forever.

questions.explanation: 正解は「Because the writer saw the owner's name and school on the ID card.」。本文に「But then I saw the name on the ID card: "Aya Mori, Sakura High School." I decided that I could not just walk away. I wanted to return it to her myself.」とあり、IDカードの名前と学校を見たことが、自分で返そうと決めた直接のきっかけである。

question_data.passage:
When I was twelve, I could not swim at all. I was afraid of deep water, so I always stayed near the edge of the pool. My friends often jumped in and laughed together, but I just watched them from the side. I really wanted to join them, but my fear was too strong.

One summer, my older sister Mika said, "I will teach you. Trust me." That sentence was the start of everything. The next morning, we went to the city pool early, before it became crowded. First, Mika told me to hold the wall and kick my legs. I felt silly, but I did it for almost an hour. My legs grew tired, yet I kept going because she stayed beside me the whole time.

After three days of kicking practice, Mika said I was ready for the next step. She held my hands and pulled me slowly through the water while I kicked. At first my body sank, and I swallowed water and coughed. I wanted to stop, but she smiled and said, "Everyone does that at the beginning." Her calm voice made me feel safe again.

A week later, something amazing happened. Mika let go of my hands without telling me. For a few seconds, I swam by myself! When I noticed she was not holding me, I panicked and stood up in the shallow water. But then I realized the truth: I had actually moved through the water alone. I was so surprised that I started to laugh.

From that day, I practiced every morning. Slowly, I could swim five meters, then ten, then across the whole pool. By the end of the summer, I jumped into the deep water with my friends for the first time. The cold water no longer scared me. Instead, it felt like freedom.

Now, when I see a child who is afraid of the water, I understand exactly how they feel. Learning to swim taught me more than a sport. It taught me that fear becomes smaller when someone believes in you and stays by your side.

(3) The writer held the wall and kicked his legs. (4) Mika pulled the writer by the hands through the water. (5) The writer jumped into the deep water with his friends. Which is the correct order?

question_data.passage:
When I was eleven, my parents finally let me keep a pet. I chose a small white rabbit from a local shop and named her Coco. I had begged for a pet for years, mostly because I wanted something soft to hold after school. At first, I thought taking care of her would be easy.

The morning after Coco arrived, I put some fresh vegetables in her cage and waited for her to eat. But she just sat in the corner and would not move. I felt worried and a little disappointed. My mother told me that Coco was probably scared because everything was new to her. She said I needed to be patient and give the rabbit time.

So every day after school, I sat quietly beside the cage without trying to touch her. I read my books out loud so she could get used to my voice. For almost two weeks, nothing seemed to change, and I began to wonder if Coco would ever trust me. Then one afternoon, while I was reading, she slowly came to the front of the cage and sniffed my fingers. I was so happy that I could hardly breathe.

After that day, Coco changed completely. She started to eat from my hand, and she would jump toward me whenever I came home. Caring for her became the best part of my day. I cleaned her cage, fed her on time, and made sure she had water, even on weekends when I wanted to sleep late.

A year later, our class had a discussion about responsibility. The teacher asked us what responsibility really meant. Many students talked about doing homework or helping at home. When it was my turn, I talked about Coco. I explained that real responsibility is not about doing something once; it is about showing up every single day, even when it is hard or boring. My classmates listened carefully, and the teacher smiled and nodded.

Coco taught me something no textbook ever could. A living thing depends on you completely, and that trust must be earned slowly through patience and care. Even now, whenever I feel like giving up on something difficult, I remember those quiet afternoons beside her cage, and I find the strength to keep going.

You are reading a short story written by a high school student, Kana, for her school's English magazine.

**The Sound of My Own Heart**

I had played the flute for three years, but I had never performed alone in front of a big audience. So when my band teacher, Mr. Sato, asked me to play a solo at the city music contest, I almost said no. My hands felt cold just thinking about it. Still, I wanted to challenge myself, so I agreed.

For two months I practiced every evening after school. Some days the music came out beautifully, and some days every note sounded wrong. The night before the contest, I could not sleep at all. I kept imagining myself forgetting the song in the middle of the stage.

On the morning of the contest, I arrived at the hall early. The building was huge, and there were players from many other schools warming up everywhere. My heart began to beat so fast that I felt sick. I sat alone in a corner and almost decided to go home.

Then my friend Mei found me. She did not say "Don't worry" or "You'll be fine." Instead, she simply sat beside me and told me that she had felt the same fear before her own piano contest last year. She said that the fear never fully disappears, but that I could carry it with me onto the stage. Hearing that, I felt a little lighter.

When my name was finally called, my legs were shaking as I walked up the steps. I lifted the flute, took one slow breath, and began. For the first few seconds I could hear nothing but my own heart. But as the melody continued, the fear slowly turned into something warm, and I started to enjoy the music. When I finished, the audience clapped loudly.

I did not win first prize that day. My score was only third place. But walking out of that hall, I understood something important. Bravery is not the absence of fear. It is choosing to play your song even while your hands are still shaking.

Eco Week at Our School (Draft for the Club Newsletter)

Last month, our Environment Club held its first Eco Week. We wanted to show students that small daily actions can make a real difference. <A> Over five days, we ran a different activity each day, and more than two hundred students joined in.

On Monday, we set up a "No-Waste Lunch" challenge. Students were asked to bring lunches with no plastic wrapping. We counted the bags of trash from the cafeteria that day. Normally the cafeteria fills about ten bags, but on Monday it filled only four. (1) This result showed that ___.

On Tuesday and Wednesday, we focused on saving energy. Club members put friendly notes near light switches and computers, reminding everyone to turn them off when leaving a room. <B> By Wednesday afternoon, several teachers told us that their classrooms felt different because students were checking the lights without being asked.

On Thursday, we held a clothing swap. Students brought clothes they no longer wore and exchanged them for items they liked. (2) More than three hundred pieces of clothing found new owners, and nothing was thrown away. <C>

On Friday, we planted twenty young trees behind the gym with help from the science teachers. (3) The students who participated in the tree planting on Friday afternoon, even though some of them had never used a shovel before in their entire lives, worked together very happily and finished the job. <D>

Eco Week taught us something important. (4) We learned that protecting the environment is not only the job of adults or scientists; it is something every student can start doing today, in small but meaningful ways.

Comments (from our teacher advisor):
- For (1): The data is clear, so finish this sentence with the conclusion the numbers support.
- For (2): I have one extra sentence to add. Find the best place for it in the newsletter.
- For (3): This sentence is too long and hard to read. Please replace it with a shorter, clearer version.
- For (4): Your ending is good, but try a shorter phrase that still keeps the main message.

Last spring, my family and I went for a walk along the Aoba River near our school. I was shocked by what I saw. Plastic bottles, empty cans, and old bags were lying everywhere on the riverbank. The water, which used to be clear when my mother was a child, now looked brown and dirty. <A> That experience made me want to do something to (1) change this situation.

Our volunteer club has decided to start a fundraising campaign called "River Smile." Our goal is to collect 100,000 yen by the end of July. <B> With this money, we will buy cleaning tools such as gloves, nets, and large garbage bags. We will also rent a small truck to carry away the heavy waste that we cannot remove by hand. <C>

You may wonder why we need money instead of simply picking up the trash ourselves. The answer is that the amount of garbage is too large for one cleanup. (2) Cleaning the river properly will take many days and the right equipment. <D> Therefore, every yen you give will be used carefully and wisely.

Please support us! You can donate at the box in front of the staff room, or join us at the river on the last Saturday of every month. (3) If everyone helps just a little, together we can make a big difference. Let's work together and (4) bring back the beautiful river that our town can be proud of.

questions.explanation: 正解は「your visit」。Comment (1)は「この動詞には目的語が必要。来場者が何を楽しむのかを加えよ」と述べている。enjoy は他動詞で目的語(名詞)を取るため、来場者が楽しむ対象を表す名詞句「your visit(あなたの来場)」が最適。「to come」は enjoy to do の形が不自然で誤り、「very much」「by yourself」は目的語ではないため不適。

questions.stem: Where is the best place to add the sticky-note sentence "Drinks and light snacks will be sold in the hallway next to the gym."?
questions.explanation: 正解は「<B>」。この文は会場全体(ジムやその隣の廊下)に関する一般的な案内であり、開催時間と場所を説明した「Twenty student teams will present their projects in the gym from 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.」の直後の<B>に置くと、場所・時間の全体案内の流れに自然につながる。<C>と<D>は「三つのエリア」の具体説明の途中であり、飲食の案内を挟むと話が中断される。<A>はテーマ提示の直後で会場説明より前のため流れが不自然。よって<B>が最適。

questions.stem: Which is the best replacement for underlined sentence (3)?
choices: You must be careful near the tables, but our members will watch every experiment closely to help you stay safe.
You must be careful when you are near the tables, and there is nothing you need to worry about because our members will watch every experiment closely and help you stay safe.
Because our members will watch every experiment closely, you must be careful when you are near the tables and help you stay safe.
You must be careful near the tables, so there is nothing you need to worry about, but our members will watch every experiment closely and help you stay safe.
questions.explanation: 正解は「You must be careful near the tables, but our members will watch every experiment closely to help you stay safe.」。Comment (3)は「二つの考えがやや不自然につながっている。もっと滑らかに書き直せ」と指摘している。元の文は「注意が必要だ」という考えと「部員が見守るので安全だ」という考えを冗長に並べている。選択肢0は「注意は必要(must be careful)」と「部員が見守って安全を助ける(to help you stay safe)」を but で簡潔につなぎ、最も滑らかで意味も保たれる。他の選択肢は接続語(and/so/because)の論理関係が不自然、または「help you stay safe」の主語がねじれており誤り。

questions.stem: The writer wants to replace underlined part (4) "have fun, learn new things, and meet students who love science" with one short phrase that sums it up, as the teacher suggested in Comment (4). Which is best?
choices: buy tickets and snacks
enjoy, learn, and connect
win the Visitors' Prize
finish your homework
questions.explanation: 正解は「enjoy, learn, and connect」。Comment (4)は「この文全体をまとめる短い語句を一つ見つけよ」と求めている。下線部(4)は「楽しむ(have fun)」「新しいことを学ぶ(learn new things)」「科学好きの生徒と出会う(meet students who love science)」の三点を述べており、これらをそれぞれ enjoy(楽しむ)・learn(学ぶ)・connect(つながる=出会う)で簡潔に要約した選択肢0が最適。「win the Visitors' Prize」「buy tickets and snacks」「finish your homework」は本文の三点の要約になっておらず不適。

You are a third-year student at Sakura High School. Your class will go on a school trip, and each student must choose one course. Read the leaflet, the request form your group filled in, and an email from your teacher, and answer the questions.

【1. Course Leaflet】

SAKURA HIGH SCHOOL TRIP — CHOOSE YOUR COURSE!
This year, the third-year trip will be held in Kyoto from October 14 to 16. On the second day, you will travel in small groups. Pick ONE of the four courses below for that day.

- Course A: Temple Walk — Visit three famous old temples and learn about their history. Walking distance: about 6 km. Cost: 1,500 yen. (Not for students who dislike long walks.)
- Course B: Craft Studio — Make your own pottery cup with a local artist. You take your cup home. Cost: 3,000 yen. Limit: 5 students per group.
- Course C: Garden & Tea — See a quiet garden and join a tea ceremony. Cost: 2,000 yen. A short kimono experience is included for free.
- Course D: River Boat — Ride a traditional wooden boat down the river and enjoy the autumn leaves. Cost: 2,500 yen. (Cancelled if it rains heavily.)

NOTE: Courses B and C are indoors. Courses A and D are mostly outdoors. Every course returns to the hotel by 4 p.m.

【2. Group Request Form (filled in by Group 3)】

We are Group 3. Each member wrote a first choice and a comment.

- Name: Mei / Choice: C / Comment: "I really want to try the kimono. I get tired after walking a lot, so an indoor course is best for me."
- Name: Ken / Choice: D / Comment: "I love nature and the river. I checked the weather and it should be sunny that day."
- Name: Aoi / Choice: B / Comment: "I want to make something I can keep. A cup I made myself would be a great memory."
- Name: Riku / Choice: A / Comment: "I enjoy walking and I'm interested in old buildings, so the temples sound perfect."
- Name: Hana / Choice: B / Comment: "I'd like to make pottery with Aoi, but I'm worried the group might be full."

【3. Email from your teacher】

From: Mr. Tanaka
To: Group 3
Subject: Your course choices

Hello Group 3,

Thank you for sending your form. Almost everything is fine, but I need two things from you before Friday.

First, Course B has a limit of five students per group, and right now only two of you chose it, so there is no problem with space. However, the artist needs the exact number of cups in advance. Please confirm whether both Aoi and Hana will join Course B, and reply with the final number.

Second, please remember that one course may be stopped because of the weather. If that happens, the student in that course must pick a new one. Talk together now and tell me a backup course for that student, just in case.

One more thing: the cost for each course must be paid in cash on the morning of the trip, so please bring the right amount.

Thank you,
Mr. Tanaka

choices: Ken and Riku
Aoi and Hana

You are reading a short story written by a student for your school's English magazine. Read it and complete the Story Outline that follows.

The Baker on Maple Street

Mr. Tanaka owned a small bakery on Maple Street, the oldest shopping street in town. Every morning at five o'clock, he turned on the lights and filled the air with the warm smell of fresh bread. He was a quiet man who rarely spoke more than a few words, but the regular customers all knew his kind heart.

One cold winter evening, a boy named Kenji walked slowly past the bakery window. He was about ten years old, and his clothes were thin and worn. He stopped and stared at the bread for a long time. Mr. Tanaka noticed him but said nothing. Instead, he placed a small loaf of bread on a paper bag near the back door, where the boy could see it, and then turned away to clean the counter. When he looked again, the bread was gone, and so was the boy.

The next evening, the same thing happened. Mr. Tanaka left a loaf by the door, and it quietly disappeared. This continued for several weeks. Mr. Tanaka never asked the boy's name, and the boy never said thank you out loud. Yet something passed between them that needed no words.

One night, a heavy snow fell, and the boy did not come. Mr. Tanaka waited, looking out the window again and again, but the street stayed empty. He began to worry. The following morning, he asked the flower shop owner next door if she had seen a thin boy in old clothes. She told him the boy lived with his sick mother in a tiny room above the laundry shop, and that they had little money.

That day, Mr. Tanaka closed his shop early. He filled a large basket with bread, milk, and warm soup, and carried it to the laundry shop. When the boy opened the door, his eyes grew wide with surprise. Mr. Tanaka simply smiled and handed him the basket. "For you and your mother," he said softly. It was the most he had ever said to the boy.

Years passed. The thin boy grew up, finished school, and became a doctor. He never forgot the baker's quiet kindness. One spring morning, a young man in a clean suit entered the bakery. Mr. Tanaka, now older and grayer, did not recognize him at first. The young man smiled and said, "You once fed a hungry boy on a winter night. I have come to thank you." Mr. Tanaka's eyes filled with tears. For once, neither of them needed many words at all.

Story Outline
- Main character: Mr. Tanaka, a baker on Maple Street
- Other character: Kenji, a poor boy who later becomes a doctor
- Setting: an old shopping street, mostly in winter
- Key events: [arrange in order]
- Theme: [about the main character]

Put the following four events into the order in which they happened.
A: Mr. Tanaka carries a basket of food to the laundry shop.
B: Mr. Tanaka leaves a loaf of bread by the back door each evening.

D: The flower shop owner tells Mr. Tanaka where the boy lives.
choices: B → D → A → C
B → A → D → C
D → B → A → C
B → D → C → A
A → B → D → C
D → A → B → C
questions.explanation: 正解は「B → D → A → C」。まず毎晩裏口にパンを置く(B)。雪の夜に少年が来ず、翌朝花屋の店主が少年の住まいを教える(D)。その後タナカ氏が籠に食料を詰めて洗濯店へ運ぶ(A)。長い年月の後、医者になった青年が礼を言いに来る(C)。この順がB→D→A→C。

questions.stem: What does the story tell us about Kenji?
choices: He grew up, became a doctor, and returned to thank Mr. Tanaka.
He thanked Mr. Tanaka loudly every evening.
He worked at the flower shop next to the bakery.
He moved to another town and was never seen again.
questions.explanation: 正解は「He grew up, became a doctor, and returned to thank Mr. Tanaka.」。本文は the thin boy grew up, finished school, and became a doctor とあり、後に a young man in a clean suit が来て I have come to thank you と述べる。よって成長して医者になり礼を言いに戻ったが正しい。声に出して礼を言わなかった(the boy never said thank you out loud)ので最初の選択肢は誤り。他も本文に根拠なし。

questions.stem: What is the main theme this story tells us about Mr. Tanaka?
choices: Hard work always leads to becoming rich.

A good business needs many loyal customers.
Family is more important than helping strangers.
questions.explanation: 正解は「Quiet, wordless kindness can change a person's life.」。物語全体は無口なタナカ氏が言葉少なに少年を助け(something passed between them that needed no words)、その親切が少年の人生を支え医者へと導いた様子を描く。よって「言葉のない静かな親切が人の人生を変える」が主題。他の選択肢は本文の焦点(無言の親切)と一致しない。

You are reading a story written by a high school student for her school's English magazine. Read the story and complete the Story Outline that follows.

The Last Lap

When I joined the school swimming team in my first year, I was the slowest swimmer in the pool. The coach, Mr. Tanaka, was famous for being strict. Older students warned me that he never smiled and that he made everyone repeat the same drills hundreds of times. On my very first day, he watched me swim one lap and said only, "Your arms are lazy. Fix them." I went home almost in tears.

For the next three months, Mr. Tanaka pushed me harder than anyone else on the team. While the faster swimmers practiced races, he kept me doing slow, boring drills by the wall. I felt embarrassed and angry. One afternoon, I finally complained, "Why do I always do the basics while everyone else gets to race?" He looked at me quietly and answered, "Because you are the one who can improve the most. I do not waste time on swimmers I have given up on." For the first time, I understood that his strictness was a kind of trust.

After that, I began to listen carefully to every word he said. I stayed late to practice the drills he gave me. Slowly, my times started to drop. By the end of my first year, I was no longer the slowest. A girl named Aya, who had joined at the same time as me, became my closest rival and my best friend. We pushed each other in every practice, and Mr. Tanaka watched us with what I now believe was hidden pride.

In my second year, our team entered the regional tournament. In my race, I was in last place at the halfway point, and I almost gave up. Then I heard Mr. Tanaka's voice from the side of the pool: "The last lap is yours. Show me what you fixed." Suddenly I remembered all those boring drills by the wall. On the final lap, I passed two swimmers and touched the wall in third place. It was not first, but it was the best race of my life.

When I climbed out of the water, Mr. Tanaka was waiting. He did not say "well done." Instead, he gave a small nod and, for the first time in two years, he smiled. Later, Aya told me that he had told the whole team I was the hardest worker he had ever coached. He never said such things to my face, but I had finally learned to read his quiet way of caring.

Now, in my third year, I am one of the team's captains. When new first-year students complain that the drills are too hard, I tell them what I once could not understand: a coach who keeps correcting you is a coach who believes in you.

Story Outline

Main character (the writer): a swimmer who grows from the slowest member into a team captain
Other people: Mr. Tanaka (the strict coach), Aya (a rival who becomes a best friend)
Key events: [arranged in time order in Question 2]
Theme: [what the writer finally understands — Question 4]

question_data.passage:
You are studying for the English test. Read the following story and complete the outline that follows.

**A Spoonful of Memory**

Mika had never paid much attention to her grandmother's cooking. When she was small, she would sit at the kitchen table, swinging her legs and waiting for dinner while her grandmother, whom everyone called Baba, hummed an old song and stirred a pot of soup. The kitchen always smelled of ginger and garlic. Back then, Mika thought the smell was just part of the house, like the wooden floor or the clock on the wall.

When Mika turned fifteen, Baba became ill and went to stay in the hospital. The house felt strangely quiet. One afternoon, Mika opened a drawer and found a small, worn notebook. Inside were dozens of recipes written in Baba's careful handwriting. Most of them she could read, but one page made her stop. At the top it said "New Year Soup," and below the list of ingredients Baba had written, "Always add the ginger last, and always cook it for someone you love."

Mika decided she wanted to make the soup. She had never cooked anything more difficult than instant noodles, so she felt nervous. She bought the ingredients after school and laid them out on the counter the way she imagined Baba would. She chopped the vegetables slowly and carefully. When she added the ginger too early by mistake, the soup turned bitter, and she had to start again. The second time, she remembered the note and added the ginger last. This time the smell that filled the kitchen was exactly the one she remembered from childhood.

That weekend, Mika carried the soup to the hospital in a warm container. Baba was thin and tired, but when she lifted the lid, her eyes brightened. "You found my notebook," she said softly, smiling. She tasted a spoonful and nodded. "It is not perfect," she said, "but it tastes like you tried. That is the secret ingredient." Mika laughed, though her eyes were wet.

Over the next month, Mika visited often, and each time she brought a new dish from the notebook. Baba would taste each one and tell Mika a story about it — which dish her own mother had taught her, which one she had made for Mika's grandfather on their wedding day. Mika began to understand that the notebook was not only a list of recipes. It was a record of her family's whole history, passed from one pair of hands to the next.

When Baba came home from the hospital in spring, she was too weak to cook. But she sat beside Mika at the counter, pointing and explaining, while Mika did the work. The kitchen filled again with the smell of ginger and garlic. Mika realized that she was no longer just a girl waiting for dinner. She had become the next person to carry the songs, the smells, and the love that lived in that little notebook.

Main characters: Mika (a fifteen-year-old girl) and her grandmother, "Baba"

Setting: Baba's house (especially the kitchen) and a hospital

Key events: [arrange in order — see Question 2]

Theme of the story: [see Question 4]

question_data.passage:
When I started my first job at a small bookstore, I was nervous and unsure of everything. On my first day, a woman named Grace introduced herself as my mentor. She had worked at the store for almost ten years and seemed to know every book on every shelf. Grace was calm and patient, and she always spoke in a quiet, steady voice that made me feel less afraid.

At first, I made many mistakes. I put books in the wrong sections and gave customers the wrong prices. One afternoon, I accidentally ordered fifty copies of a book instead of five. I felt terrible and expected Grace to be angry. Instead, she just laughed gently and said, "Everyone makes mistakes when they are learning. I once ordered two hundred copies of a cookbook nobody wanted." Her kindness made me relax, and I promised myself I would try harder.

Grace taught me more than how to use the cash register. She showed me how to listen to customers and help them find exactly what they needed. "A good bookseller doesn't just sell books," she often said. "We help people discover stories that change their lives." I watched how she remembered the names of regular customers and the kinds of books they liked. Slowly, I began to do the same.

One busy Saturday, a young boy came in looking for a book about space. He was shy and could barely speak. Grace was helping someone else, so I decided to help him by myself. I remembered everything Grace had taught me. I asked the boy gentle questions and finally found a beautiful book about the planets. His eyes lit up with joy, and his mother thanked me warmly. When Grace saw what had happened, she smiled and said, "You're becoming a real bookseller now."

A few months later, Grace told me she was leaving to open her own bookstore in another town. I felt sad, but I also felt grateful. On her last day, she gave me a small notebook. Inside, she had written all her best advice about books and customers. "Now it's your turn to teach someone new," she wrote on the first page. I held the notebook tightly and promised I would.

Today, I still work at the same bookstore, but now I am the senior staff member. Last week, a nervous young man started his first job here, and I introduced myself as his mentor. I remembered how scared I had felt on my own first day, and I spoke to him in a calm, quiet voice, just like Grace once did. I know I have a lot to teach him, and I am ready.

Story Outline:
- Main character: a new worker at a bookstore who grows from a nervous beginner into a confident mentor.
- Grace: an experienced mentor who guides the main character with patience and kindness.
- Key events: starting the job, making mistakes, learning from Grace, helping a customer alone, Grace leaving, becoming a mentor.
- Theme: what the main character learns about growth and passing on kindness.

question_data.passage:
The Blue Bicycle

When Mika moved to the small town of Hadano at the age of seven, she felt lonely and afraid. On her first morning there, a boy named Ren knocked on her door. He had bright eyes and a friendly smile, and he was holding two ice creams. "I saw the moving truck," he said. "Welcome! This one is for you." From that day, Mika and Ren became close friends.

They lived next door to each other, and they did everything together. Ren was always cheerful and brave, while Mika was quiet and careful. Ren loved adventures. He often led Mika up the hill behind their houses to watch the sunset. Mika was sometimes nervous about climbing so high, but Ren always waited for her and held her hand. "Don't worry," he would say. "I won't let you fall."

One summer, when they were ten, Ren taught Mika how to ride a bicycle. She fell many times and scraped her knees, but Ren never laughed at her. He ran beside her, holding the back of the seat, until at last she could ride alone. When she finally rode across the schoolyard by herself, Ren cheered loudly and jumped into the air. That blue bicycle became Mika's most precious thing.

The following spring, Ren's family had to move far away because of his father's job. On the day he left, Ren gave Mika a small, hand-drawn map. "This shows the way to the top of our hill," he said quietly. "Keep it safe. One day, I'll come back, and we'll watch the sunset there together again." Mika tried hard not to cry. She kept the map in a wooden box for many years.

Ten years passed. Mika was now a university student, still living in Hadano. She rarely climbed the hill anymore, but she never threw the map away. One autumn afternoon, while she was riding her old blue bicycle through the park, someone called her name. She stopped and turned around. A tall young man was standing there, smiling. His eyes were just as bright as she remembered. It was Ren.

"You still have that bicycle!" he laughed. Mika could hardly speak. They sat on a bench and talked for hours, just like in the old days. Ren explained that he had returned to Hadano to study at the same university. He had thought about Mika often, and he had kept his own copy of the map all this time.

That evening, the two friends climbed the hill together, just as they had promised long ago. As the orange sun sank slowly behind the mountains, Mika realized something important. The years apart had not broken their friendship; they had only made it stronger. Some bonds, she understood, can survive any distance and any amount of time.

- Mika: a girl who moves to Hadano; (A) ____
- Ren: Mika's neighbor and best friend; (B) ____

Key events (in the order they happened): (C)

Theme about Mika: (D) ____

question_data.passage:
Why Your Brain Needs Sleep to Learn

Sleep is not just rest; the brain is busy while we sleep, and that activity helps us learn. When you study, your brain forms weak connections that are easily lost. To keep new information, the brain changes them into stronger ones. This is called memory consolidation, and most of it happens during sleep, not while you are awake.

In deep sleep, mainly in the first half of the night, the brain replays the facts you learned and moves them to long-term memory; this helps remember facts, dates, and vocabulary. Later, REM sleep gets longer; the brain looks for patterns, helping with solving problems and creative thinking.

In one study, two groups learned the same word pairs. One slept; one stayed awake. The next day the group that slept remembered far more, though both studied the same time.

Advice: sleep before a test beats studying all night; review just before sleeping; keep a regular sleep schedule.

You are preparing a presentation for your class about how music affects the human brain and mood. You found the following article and made some slides based on it.

Music and the Brain: Why a Good Song Can Change How You Feel

Almost everyone has had the experience of feeling better after listening to a favorite song. For a long time, this feeling was treated as a simple matter of taste. In recent years, however, brain scientists have begun to explain what actually happens inside our heads when we listen to music, and the findings are surprising.

When we hear a song we enjoy, the brain releases a chemical called dopamine. Dopamine is often called the "reward chemical" because the brain produces it when we eat tasty food or receive good news. Studies using brain scanners show that the strongest release of dopamine does not always happen at the most exciting moment of a song. Instead, the brain produces the most dopamine in the few seconds just before a favorite part arrives, when the listener is expecting it. In other words, the feeling of pleasure comes largely from prediction. This is why a song that is too simple, with no surprises at all, can feel boring, while a song that is completely unpredictable can feel uncomfortable. The most enjoyable music sits between these two extremes.

Music also affects the body. Slow music with a steady beat can lower the heart rate and reduce the level of stress hormones in the blood. For this reason, some hospitals now play calm music before operations to help patients relax. Fast music with a strong beat tends to have the opposite effect, raising energy and making physical movement feel easier. This is one reason many people listen to fast songs while exercising; researchers have found that runners who listen to fast music often run a little longer before they feel tired.

Another important point is timing. Scientists have learned that the effect of music depends on when it is used. Listening to calm music right before sleep can help people fall asleep faster, but listening to the same calm music in the morning may simply make a person feel sleepy and slow. Energetic music helps most when a person needs to start a difficult task, but it can make relaxation harder if it is played late at night.

Memory is connected to music as well. A song that a person heard during an important moment in the past can bring back strong emotions and clear memories years later. Doctors have used this discovery to help older patients with memory problems. When these patients hear songs from their youth, they sometimes remember names, places, and events that they could not recall before. The music seems to open a door to memories that are still there but hard to reach.

What does all of this mean for daily life? The science suggests that we can use music as a simple tool. By choosing the right kind of music at the right time, we can calm ourselves, give ourselves energy, or reconnect with our past. Music is not only entertainment; it is also a gentle and natural way to shape how we feel.

You are preparing a presentation about how habits are formed. You found the following article and made slides based on it.

Have you ever noticed that you do certain things almost without thinking? Maybe you check your phone the moment you wake up, or you turn on music as soon as you enter your room. These automatic actions are called habits, and scientists have studied for many years how they form in our brains.

A habit is built through a simple loop with three parts: a cue, a routine, and a reward. A cue is a signal that tells your brain to start a certain behavior. The routine is the action itself. The reward is the good feeling that follows. For example, the smell of coffee (cue) may lead you to drink a cup (routine), which makes you feel awake and happy (reward). When this loop repeats again and again, the brain learns to connect the cue with the reward, and the routine becomes automatic.

Why does the brain do this? The answer is energy. Thinking carefully about every action uses a lot of mental effort. By turning repeated actions into habits, the brain saves energy for more important decisions. This is helpful, but it also means that bad habits can form just as easily as good ones, because the brain does not judge whether a habit is healthy or not.

Researchers once believed that it takes exactly 21 days to build a new habit, but recent studies have shown that this number is a myth. One well-known study followed 96 people who tried to form a new habit, such as eating fruit at lunch or going for a walk. The results showed that the time needed ranged widely from 18 days to 254 days, with an average of about 66 days. Importantly, missing the behavior once in a while did not stop the habit from forming. This finding suggests that being perfect is not necessary; what matters most is steady repetition over time.

The study also revealed that habits form fastest when the behavior is tied to an existing daily event. This is called "habit stacking." If you want to start flossing your teeth, attaching it to something you already do every day, like brushing your teeth, makes the new behavior much easier to remember. The existing action works as a reliable cue, so you do not have to depend on memory or motivation alone.

Breaking a bad habit, however, is harder than building a new one. Scientists explain that the old loop does not disappear from the brain; it only becomes weaker. The most effective method is not to remove the cue but to keep the same cue and reward while changing the routine in the middle. For instance, if you eat snacks (routine) when you feel stressed (cue) in order to relax (reward), you can replace the snacks with a short walk that also helps you relax. In this way, the cue and the reward stay the same, but the unhealthy action is replaced by a healthier one.

Understanding this science gives us a practical message: habits are not signs of weak willpower. They are patterns the brain creates to make life easier, and by designing our cues and rewards carefully, we can shape them in our favor.

You are preparing a presentation about how curiosity helps people learn. Read the following article and complete the slides.

**The Power of Curiosity**

Have you ever wondered why you can easily remember a strange fact you came across by accident, yet forget information you tried hard to memorize for a test? Scientists who study the brain believe the answer is curiosity. Curiosity is the strong desire to know or learn something. When we feel curious, our brains become ready to take in new information, and learning happens more naturally.

A team of researchers in California ran an interesting experiment. They showed volunteers a long list of trivia questions, such as "What is the only animal that cannot jump?" For each question, the volunteers reported how curious they were to learn the answer. Then the answers were shown one by one. Two weeks later, the researchers tested the volunteers' memory. The results were clear: people remembered far more answers to the questions that had made them highly curious than answers to the questions they found boring. Curiosity, it seemed, acted like glue that fixed information in the mind.

But how does this happen inside the brain? Brain scans during the experiment showed that when a person feels strong curiosity, a chemical called dopamine is released. Dopamine is often linked to feelings of pleasure and reward. The same chemical that makes us enjoy delicious food or exciting games is released when we are eager to learn. In this curious state, a memory area of the brain called the hippocampus becomes more active. As a result, not only the answer the person wanted, but also other information that happens to appear at the same moment, is remembered better. In other words, curiosity opens a "memory window," and whatever passes through it during that short period tends to stick.

This finding has useful lessons for students. First, instead of forcing yourself to study a topic you find dull, try to turn it into a question you genuinely want to answer. Asking "Why?" or "What would happen if?" can switch on your curiosity before you begin. Second, timing matters. Because the memory window stays open only briefly, it is wise to study the most difficult material right after your curiosity has been triggered, not hours later. Third, mixing subjects can help. If a boring task is studied close to a fascinating one, the excitement from the interesting topic may carry over and support the harder learning.

Of course, curiosity alone is not magic. Researchers warn that effort and repetition are still necessary for deep learning. Curiosity gives learning a powerful start, but practice keeps the knowledge alive. Still, understanding how curiosity works gives every learner a simple, free tool. The next time you feel that small spark of "I want to know," do not ignore it. Follow it, and let your brain do what it does best.

---

- Mix boring and interesting subjects

Slide 6: Final Message

You are preparing a presentation for your English class about why people forget. You found the following article and made some slides.

**Why We Forget**

Many people think of forgetting as a kind of failure. When you cannot remember a friend's name or where you left your keys, it feels as though your brain has broken down. But scientists who study memory now believe that forgetting is not a flaw. Instead, it is a normal and even useful part of how a healthy brain works.

Every day your brain takes in a huge amount of information. If you remembered every single thing you ever saw, heard, or read, your mind would soon be filled with useless details. Forgetting helps you clear away information you no longer need, so that the memories that truly matter can stand out. In this way, forgetting acts like a filter that keeps your thinking clear.

Memory does not stay fixed once it is formed. A new memory is fragile at first and must be made stronger through a process called consolidation, which happens mostly while you sleep. During deep sleep, the brain replays the events of the day and decides which ones to keep. Memories that are used again and connected to other knowledge become firm. Memories that are never used slowly fade. This is why a fact you study once and never review is usually gone within a week.

Forgetting also helps you grow. Old information can sometimes get in the way of new learning. For example, if you move to a new house, you must forget your old address before the new one feels natural. When the brain lets go of outdated memories, it makes room for fresh, more useful ones. People who can update their memories easily tend to adapt better to change.

Researchers have found that sleep and forgetting are deeply linked. In one study, two groups of students learned a list of new words. One group slept for eight hours before being tested, while the other group stayed awake. The group that slept remembered the important words far better, but they had also dropped many of the unimportant ones. The waking group held on to more random details but performed worse overall. The scientists concluded that sleep does not simply store everything; it sorts memories, keeping the valuable ones and removing the rest.

So how can you make the memories you care about last? The advice from researchers is simple. First, get enough deep sleep, because that is when sorting happens. Second, review important material more than once, spreading your study over several days rather than cramming it all at once. Third, connect new facts to things you already know, since linked memories are far harder to lose. Forgetting, then, is not your enemy. It is the quiet partner of memory, working in the background so that what matters most stays with you.

Slide 3: Advice for Lasting Memory

- Link new facts to old knowledge
